title: How do Java records relate to OOP — immutable, auto-generates equals/hashCode/toString, final, cannot extend — and when is a record NOT suitable (mutable state, inheritance, JPA entities)?

s1_definition.profdef: A Java `record` (Java 16) is an immutable data carrier class that auto-generates: canonical constructor, accessor methods (name() not getName()), `equals()` based on ALL components, `hashCode()` based on ALL components, and `toString()` showing all components. Records are implicitly `final` (cannot be extended) and their fields are implicitly `private final`. Records enforce OOP's ENCAPSULATION (immutable fields, no setters) and VALUE SEMANTICS (two records with same field values ARE equal). Records are NOT suitable when: (1) you need MUTABLE state (setters — records don't have them), (2) you need INHERITANCE hierarchy (records are final), (3) JPA entities (require no-arg constructor + mutable fields for dirty checking — records are immutable + have no no-arg constructor).
s1_definition.analogy: A record is like a SEALED bank receipt: once printed (constructed), it CANNOT be modified. Two receipts with the same transaction details ARE considered identical (equals). The receipt automatically shows all details (toString). You cannot create a "special receipt" subclass (final). Records are perfect for DTOs: `TradeConfirmation(tradeId, symbol, amount, timestamp)` — data that flows between layers, never modified.
s1_definition.oneliner: record = immutable, final, auto equals/hashCode/toString, no setters, no inheritance. Perfect for: DTOs, value objects, map keys. NOT for: JPA entities, mutable domain objects, class hierarchies.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Java `record` (Java 16) is an immutable data carrier class that auto-generates: canonical constructor, accessor methods (name() not getName()), `equals()` based on ALL components, `hashCode()` based on ALL components, and `toString()` showing all components. Records are implicitly `final` (cannot be extended) and their fields are implicitly `private final`. Records enforce OOP's ENCAPSULATION (immutable fields, no setters) and VALUE SEMANTICS (two records with same field values ARE equal). Records are NOT suitable when: (1) you need MUTABLE state (setters — records don't have them), (2) you need INHERITANCE hierarchy (records are final), (3) JPA entities (require no-arg constructor + mutable fields for dirty checking — records are immutable + have no no-arg constructor).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A record is like a SEALED bank receipt: once printed (constructed), it CANNOT be modified. Two receipts with the same transaction details ARE considered identical (equals). The receipt automatically shows all details (toString). You cannot create a "special receipt" subclass (final). Records are perfect for DTOs: `TradeConfirmation(tradeId, symbol, amount, timestamp)` — data that flows between layers, never modified.

**One line to remember:** record = immutable, final, auto equals/hashCode/toString, no setters, no inheritance. Perfect for: DTOs, value objects, map keys. NOT for: JPA entities, mutable domain objects, class hierarchies.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The bank's trade system has 15 DTO classes, each with 40+ lines of boilerplate** (constructor, getters, equals, hashCode, toString). A developer forgot to include `amount` in `equals()` for TradeConfirmation — two different trades with different amounts were treated as duplicates in a HashSet, causing a Rs.2 crore reconciliation error. The fix: replace all DTOs with records. `record TradeConfirmation(String tradeId, String symbol, BigDecimal amount, LocalDateTime timestamp) {}` — 1 line. Equals includes ALL components automatically. Bug impossible.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** `record TradeConfirmation(tradeId, symbol, amount, status, timestamp) {}` — compiler generates: private final fields, constructor, 5 accessor methods, equals, hashCode, toString. 1 line → ~50 lines of equivalent code.

**Step 2 — Encapsulation.** `tc.tradeId = "X"` doesn't compile — fields are private final. No setters exist. Once created, the record CANNOT be modified. True immutability.

**Step 3 — Value semantics.** Two TradeConfirmation objects with identical tradeId + symbol + amount + status + timestamp ARE equal. HashSet correctly deduplicates. HashMap correctly looks up. No missing-field-in-equals bug possible.

**Step 4 — Validation.** Compact constructor: `public TradeConfirmation { if (tradeId == null) throw IAE; }` — validates BEFORE fields are assigned. No invalid records can exist.

**Step 5 — NOT for JPA.** JPA entities need: no-arg constructor (records don't have), setters (records are immutable), non-final class (records are final). Use records for DTOs that carry data between layers. Use regular classes for JPA entities that are persisted and modified.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ RECORD = 1 LINE → 50 LINES OF CODE ═══

  record Trade(String tradeId, String symbol, BigDecimal amount) {}

  Auto-generates:
  ├─ private final String tradeId;     ← encapsulated + immutable
  ├─ private final String symbol;
  ├─ private final BigDecimal amount;
  ├─ Trade(String, String, BigDecimal) ← canonical constructor
  ├─ String tradeId()                  ← accessor (NOT getTradeId!)
  ├─ String symbol()
  ├─ BigDecimal amount()
  ├─ equals(Object) → ALL components   ← value semantics
  ├─ hashCode() → ALL components       ← works in HashMap/HashSet
  └─ toString() → ALL components       ← "Trade[tradeId=...,symbol=...,amount=...]"

  ═══ WHEN TO USE / NOT USE ═══

  (Recommended) USE records for:                (Avoid) DON'T use records for:
  ├─ DTOs (TradeResponse)            ├─ JPA entities (need no-arg + setters)
  ├─ Value objects (Money)           ├─ Mutable domain objects (Account.setBalance)
  ├─ Map keys (CompositeKey)         ├─ Inheritance hierarchies (records are final)
  ├─ Event payloads (TradeEvent)     ├─ Spring beans (need proxying → non-final)
  └─ API responses                   └─ Hibernate entities
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Java records enforce OOP principles automatically: encapsulation through private final fields with no setters (true immutability), and value semantics through auto-generated equals and hashCode based on ALL components. One line `record Trade(String tradeId, String symbol, BigDecimal amount) {}` replaces 50+ lines of POJO boilerplate — constructor, getters, equals, hashCode, toString. Records are implicitly final (cannot be extended) and their components are implicitly private final.

In my banking service, replacing a hand-written TradeConfirmation POJO with a record eliminated a Rs.2 crore bug: the developer had forgotten to include `amount` in equals() — two trades with different amounts were treated as duplicates in a HashSet. Records auto-include ALL components in equals — this bug is STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE with records. The compact constructor validates at creation time: null tradeId and negative amounts are rejected before the record is constructed.

Records are NOT suitable for JPA entities (need no-arg constructor, mutable fields for dirty checking, non-final class for proxying), mutable domain objects (no setters — records are immutable), or inheritance hierarchies (records are final). Records ARE perfect for DTOs (TradeResponse), value objects (Money, Address), composite Map keys (accountId + date), and event payloads (TradeExecutedEvent). In Spring Boot: use records for request/response DTOs and configuration properties (@ConfigurationProperties with record). Use regular classes for @Entity.
